123	\label{sec:method:taxonomy}

Our method occupies the Per-token $\times$ Coupled cell (organizational framework). Empty cells represent unexplored combinations; their relative merit is an open question.}
130	\label{tab:taxonomy}

132	\begin{tabular}{lccc}

141	
142	\paragraph{Correction granularity.}
143	\emph{Static} methods~\cite{xu2025spon} learn a fixed bias vector per layer that does not depend on the input token.
144	\emph{Per-token} methods~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward,akhauri2024shadowllm,szatkowski2024d2dmoe} produce a unique mask for each input position, conditioning on the token's hidden state at each layer.
145	
146	\paragraph{Training signal coupling.}
147	\emph{Decomposed} objectives (BCE) treat each neuron independently, optimizing per-element classification against an oracle mask.
148	\emph{Intermediate} objectives (MSE on hidden states) capture local coupling within a single layer but not end-to-end output effects.
149	\emph{Coupled} objectives (KL on output distribution) propagate gradients through the full forward pass; each mask decision's gradient reflects its joint effect with all other masks on the final distribution.
150	
151	SPON~\cite{xu2025spon} distills a per-layer bias via KL but cannot adapt to per-input neuron importance (static $\times$ coupled).
152	DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} and FastForward~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} achieve per-token granularity but use BCE, where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.
153	D2DMoE~\cite{szatkowski2024d2dmoe} provides intermediate coupling (MSE on hidden states) but not end-to-end output effects.
154	Our method combines per-token prediction with coupled KL training (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}), propagating gradients through all downstream layers.
155	We define \emph{coupling alignment} as whether the training loss optimizes a quantity that composes across layers.
156	KL on output logits directly optimizes next-token prediction loss, which does not suffer from error composition; per-layer MSE minimizes reconstruction error independently at each layer, but layer-wise optima do not compose---a mask minimizing FFN output error at layer $\ell$ may amplify errors in layers $\ell{+}1 \ldots L$.

\subsection{Two-Dimensional Taxonomy of Sparsity Prediction Methods}
\label{sec:method:taxonomy}

We organize prior work along two axes: \emph{correction granularity} (how the mask adapts to input) and \emph{training signal coupling} (whether the objective captures inter-neuron dependencies).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Taxonomy of learned sparsity prediction methods along correction granularity (rows) and training signal coupling (columns). Our method occupies the Per-token $\times$ Coupled cell (organizational framework). Empty cells represent unexplored combinations; their relative merit is an open question.}
\label{tab:taxonomy}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
 & Decomposed (BCE) & Intermediate (MSE) & Coupled (KL) \\
\midrule
Static & --- & --- & SPON \\
Per-token & DejaVu, FastForward & ShadowLLM, D2DMoE & \textbf{Ours} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Correction granularity.}
\emph{Static} methods~\cite{xu2025spon} learn a fixed bias vector per layer that does not depend on the input token.
\emph{Per-token} methods~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward,akhauri2024shadowllm,szatkowski2024d2dmoe} produce a unique mask for each input position, conditioning on the token's hidden state at each layer.

\paragraph{Training signal coupling.}
\emph{Decomposed} objectives (BCE) treat each neuron independently, optimizing per-element classification against an oracle mask.
\emph{Intermediate} objectives (MSE on hidden states) capture local coupling within a single layer but not end-to-end output effects.
\emph{Coupled} objectives (KL on output distribution) propagate gradients through the full forward pass; each mask decision's gradient reflects its joint effect with all other masks on the final distribution.

SPON~\cite{xu2025spon} distills a per-layer bias via KL but cannot adapt to per-input neuron importance (static $\times$ coupled).
DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} and FastForward~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} achieve per-token granularity but use BCE, where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.
D2DMoE~\cite{szatkowski2024d2dmoe} provides intermediate coupling (MSE on hidden states) but not end-to-end output effects.
Our method combines per-token prediction with coupled KL training (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}), propagating gradients through all downstream layers.
We define \emph{coupling alignment} as whether the training loss optimizes a quantity that composes across layers.

\paragraph{Relaxation, Divergence, and SPON.}
Replacing Gumbel-Sigmoid with STE~\cite{bengio2013ste} degrades PPL from 11.79 to 15.77 (+33.8\%). % exp_id: ste_baseline_s42
Forward KL outperforms JSD (+6.4\%) and reverse KL (+8.6\%), consistent with mode-covering preserving important neurons~\cite{gu2024minillm}. % exp_id: jsd_ablation_s42, reverse_kl_ablation_s42
Adding SPON~\cite{xu2025spon} bias correction contributes 2.4\% relative (Appendix~\ref{app:spon}). % exp_id: spon_2048_s42, mvp_kl_norm_v2_s42

lines: -Replacing Gumbel-Sigmoid with STE~\cite{bengio2013ste} degrades PPL from 11.79 to 15.77 (+33.8\%). % exp_id: ste_baseline_s42
-Forward KL outperforms JSD (+6.4\%) and reverse KL (+8.6\%), consistent with mode-covering preserving important neurons~\cite{gu2024minillm}. % exp_id: jsd_ablation_s42, reverse_kl_ablation_s42
+At 50\%, replacing Gumbel-Sigmoid with STE~\cite{bengio2013ste} degrades PPL from 11.79 to 15.77 (+33.8\%). % exp_id: ste_baseline_s42

+Forward KL outperforms JSD (+6.4\%) and reverse KL (+8.6\%) at 50\%, consistent with mode-covering preserving important neurons~\cite{gu2024minillm}. % exp_id: jsd_ablation_s42, reverse_kl_ablation_s42

+At 30\%, the coupled-loss advantage persists: forward KL (8.82) and JSD (8.88) achieve near-identical PPL, both outperforming reverse KL (9.31), with all three dramatically better than MSE (20.43). % exp_id: kl30_ablation_s42, jsd30_ablation_s42, rkl30_ablation_s42, mse30_uniform_s42
+The near-equivalence of forward KL and JSD at 30\% suggests that the specific divergence measure matters less than whether the loss couples mask decisions through the output distribution.
Adding SPON~\cite{xu2025spon} bias correction contributes 2.4\% relative (Appendix~\ref{app:spon}). % exp_id: spon_2048_s42, mvp_kl_norm_v2_s42

+At 30\% sparsity, the STE limitation becomes more severe: binary gradients produce tied sigmoid scores, causing the threshold-based mask to retain far more neurons than the target (effective model-level sparsity: 20.8\% vs.\ target 30\%).
+This confirms that Gumbel-Sigmoid's continuous relaxation is necessary for reliable sparsity enforcement under Lagrangian control. % exp_id: ste_30pct_sparsity_failure
BCE+Gumbel (32.22) underperforms plain BCE (27.97), indicating a negative interaction: stochastic relaxation degrades BCE's binary target signal but benefits KL's end-to-end gradient flow.

BCE+STE confirms this asymmetry: PPL 60.54 ($5.1\times$ KL+Gumbel), with downstream collapse (MMLU 29\%, WG 52\%); KL's output-level objective absorbs relaxation noise while BCE's neuron-level objective amplifies it. % exp_id: bce_gumbel_no_penalty_s42, bce_gumbel_lagrangian_isolation, eval_bce_v3_s42, bce_ste_s42

226:\label{app:mse_config}

228-The MSE predictor uses identical architecture (two-layer MLP, bottleneck $d_b{=}128$), training data (WikiText-103, 1000 steps), optimizer (AdamW, lr=$1{\times}10^{-3}$, weight decay $1{\times}10^{-2}$, cosine decay), Gumbel-Sigmoid mask generation ($\tau$: $1.0 \to 0.1$), and adaptive Lagrangian sparsity control as the KL and BCE predictors.
229-The only difference is the loss target: per-layer $\|\mathbf{W}_d^{(\ell)}(\tilde{\mathbf{m}}^{(\ell)} \odot \mathbf{g}^{(\ell)} \odot \mathbf{x}^{(\ell)} \mathbf{W}_u^{(\ell)}) - \mathbf{y}_{\text{dense}}^{(\ell)}\|_2^2$, replacing the end-to-end KL divergence.
230-This controlled comparison isolates the effect of coupling alignment: all three predictors see identical data in identical order with identical architectures; only the loss function differs. % exp_id: mse30_uniform_s42, mse50_uniform_s42

\section{Introduction}

SwiGLU feed-forward networks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} in modern LLMs exhibit high contextual sparsity: at any given token, a large fraction of FFN neurons contribute negligibly to the output.
SwiGLU's gated activation makes prediction challenging: importance depends on both gate and up-projection values, a target that magnitude-based methods handle suboptimally.
Learned sparsity predictors~\cite{liu2023dejavu,gautam2026fastforward} exploit this property by training small networks to anticipate which neurons are important, but they universally rely on binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, treating each neuron as an independent classification target.
Yet at inference, sparsity budgets are allocated globally: the TEAL (training-free activation sparsity;~\citealp{liu2025teal}) top-$k$ mechanism ranks all neurons across all layers and retains only those above a model-wide threshold.
This mismatch between per-neuron training and global inference allocation has not been formally analyzed.
While MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} applies KL-based mask optimization, it targets static N:M weight sparsity; activation sparsity requires masks that generalize to unseen inputs, vary per token, and coordinate across layers through global allocation.

Gradient analysis reveals a structural asymmetry: BCE's gradient $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} / \partial s_j = \sigma(s_j) - m_j^*$ depends only on neuron $j$, while under KL divergence, the gradient couples each neuron to all others through the downstream Jacobian (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}).
KL's coupled gradients discover neuron importance patterns that diverge 68\% from magnitude-based masks (per-layer Jaccard 32\%).
A target-swap ablation confirms that these discovered mask targets are the proximate quality driver at inference: BCE trained on KL-derived targets reproduces KL quality (max $\Delta$$\leq$0.79pp at 50\%, s42), while magnitude-trained BCE achieves 28.13$\pm$0.20. Gradient coupling remains necessary at the discovery stage.

We instantiate a lightweight predictor (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base) trained with forward KL and Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}.
At 30\% sparsity under uniform allocation, the predictor reduces TEAL's perplexity by 14.5\% at matched sparsity (8.81 vs.\ 10.30 at 28.5\%) with stable downstream (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed); global top-$k$ amplifies cross-seed variance ($7.3\times$).
At 50\%, the perplexity advantage widens (50\% over TEAL), but downstream reasoning collapses regardless of method.

Cross-architecture evaluation on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} (3-seed) confirms the PPL advantage ($-$17.3\%) with robust commonsense gains but tied MMLU; preliminary evaluation on Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} shows consistent PPL improvement but reasoning decline (GSM8K $-$20pp, MMLU $-$2.8pp).
This paper is primarily an empirical study: we do not propose a new architecture or algorithm, but rather characterize how the training objective shapes sparsity prediction quality, and analyze interactions between allocation strategy, sparsity level, and model scale. Wall-clock speedup requires sparse kernel support not addressed here (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item A target-swap ablation confirms that KL's discovered mask targets drive inference-stage quality; gradient coupling remains necessary at the discovery stage (\S\ref{sec:mask_analysis}).
\item These mask patterns render post-hoc compensation (+67.2M params) redundant at both tested sparsity levels (\S\ref{sec:isocompute}).
\item Empirical evidence that per-layer coupling (MSE) degrades below training-free baselines, demonstrating the necessity of output-aligned training for composable masks (\S\ref{sec:method:taxonomy}).
\item Preliminary analysis of allocation-to-downstream interactions at 7--14B: non-monotonic allocation preference at 8B and scale-dependent effects at 14B (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Training-Free Activation Sparsity.}
TEAL~\cite{liu2025teal} applies global top-$k$ selection by activation magnitude and achieves 40--50\% sparsity with no training cost.
CATS~\cite{lee2024cats} adapts per-layer thresholds for SiLU/SwiGLU activations; R-Sparse~\cite{zhang2025rsparse} predicts sparsity from rank-aware SVD projections; DIP~\cite{federici2025dip} combines dynamic input pruning with cache-aware masking; SparseInfer~\cite{shin2025sparseinfer} predicts activation sparsity patterns from attention outputs without additional training.
Wang et al.~\cite{wang2025dynamicsparse} address the interaction between dynamic sparsity and quantization with zigzag-patterned weight layouts.
Dhar et al.~\cite{dhar2024activation} characterize activation sparsity opportunities across architectures, showing that SwiGLU models exhibit lower natural sparsity than ReLU counterparts.
OWL~\cite{yin2024owl} determines non-uniform per-layer sparsity ratios based on activation outlier distribution for weight pruning.
All training-free methods determine masks from fixed statistics or input-independent criteria, while our predictor generates \emph{input-dependent} masks trained to minimize output-distribution divergence.

\paragraph{Predictor-Based Contextual Sparsity.}
DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} introduced learned sparsity predictors trained via BCE to classify each neuron independently.
ShadowLLM~\cite{akhauri2024shadowllm} uses attention-based routing with per-layer MSE supervision for intermediate coupling within each layer but without end-to-end gradient signal.
FastForward~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} adds a 67.2M-parameter compensation network using BCE for mask prediction, adding inference latency.
SVD-CSP~\cite{serbin2026svdcsp} compresses sparsity predictors via SVD decomposition for reduced predictor overhead.
PowerInfer~\cite{song2024powerinfer} exploits power-law activation frequencies for GPU--CPU scheduling.
MaskLLM~\cite{fang2024maskllm} shares the principle of frozen weights + learnable masks + KL training, but the two methods differ in three fundamental ways.
First, \emph{sparsity type}: MaskLLM targets N:M semi-structured \emph{weight} sparsity (static 2:4 patterns), while we target \emph{activation} sparsity (dynamic per-token masks). Weight masks are fixed after training; our masks vary with each input token.
Second, \emph{mask generation}: MaskLLM's masks are directly learnable parameters (one per weight group) selected via Gumbel-Softmax; we train a predictor network that generates masks at inference from hidden states for input-dependent decisions.
Third, \emph{allocation}: MaskLLM optimizes within fixed N:M groups where KL coupling operates only within small local neighborhoods; our masks are ranked under a global top-$k$ budget across all layers, creating long-range dependencies that per-neuron BCE cannot capture and amplifying the coupled-vs-decomposed gap.
All prior predictor-based methods for activation sparsity use decomposed (BCE) or intermediate (MSE) objectives where each neuron's gradient is independent of other mask states.
Our contribution is primarily empirical: we observe that a coupled KL objective propagates gradients through all downstream layers and quantify when this matters for global allocation quality.

\paragraph{Static Bias Correction.}
SPON (Spontaneous Neurons;~\citealp{xu2025spon}) learns input-independent bias vectors via closed-form KL minimization per layer, absorbed into weights at deployment.
Our method is fundamentally different: a per-token contextual predictor trained end-to-end across all layers that produces input-dependent masks.
SPON solves a static per-layer problem; we solve a global dynamic prediction problem. The two are weakly correlated (cosine similarity 0.196, $R^2$=0.038; \S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\paragraph{Activation Function Engineering.}
ReLU Strikes Back~\cite{mirzadeh2024relu} replaces SiLU with ReLU for $>$90\% natural sparsity; TurboSparse~\cite{song2024turbosparse} and ProSparse~\cite{song2025prosparse} engineer extreme sparsity through activation modifications; the Sparsing Law~\cite{luo2024sparsinglaw} formalizes how activation density increases with training compute.
MiniTron~\cite{muralidharan2024minitron} combines structured pruning with distillation but modifies architecture permanently.
Haziza et al.~\cite{haziza2025accelerating} demonstrate 2:4 semi-structured activation sparsity with hardware-native acceleration, complementing our unstructured approach.
All require retraining or weight modification; our method is a plug-in predictor on \emph{unmodified} SwiGLU models.

\paragraph{Weight Pruning, Distillation, and Routing.}
Wanda~\cite{sun2024wanda}, SparseGPT~\cite{frantar2023sparsegpt}, and SliceGPT~\cite{ashkboos2024slicegpt} produce static weight masks via one-shot or structured pruning; Polar Sparsity~\cite{shrestha2025polar} scales contextual sparsity to batched inference by shifting focus from MLP to attention head sparsity.
Switch Transformers~\cite{fedus2022switch} and Mixture-of-Depths~\cite{raposo2024mod} achieve conditional computation through learned routing.
KL-based distillation~\cite{kim2016sequencekd,sanh2019distilbert,gu2024minillm,agarwal2024gkd,ko2024distillm} trains compact students; SparseLoRA~\cite{khaki2025sparselora} exploits contextual sparsity for fine-tuning.
We apply the KL principle to train a sparsity predictor on unmodified dense models, using Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling~\cite{maddison2017concrete,louizos2018l0} for differentiable discrete mask optimization.

\paragraph{MoE Routing and Gated Sparsity.}
Expert Choice routing~\cite{zhou2022expertchoice} lets each expert select its top-$k$ tokens under a fixed capacity budget, a global allocation perspective that parallels TEAL's neuron-level global top-$k$.
D2D-MoE~\cite{szatkowski2024d2dmoe} converts dense SwiGLU layers into dynamic-$k$ MoE by exploiting the same activation sparsity we target, but restructures the network into discrete experts rather than predicting masks on the original architecture.
MoNE~\cite{cheng2025mone} applies neuron-granular top-$k$ selection within each MoE expert during pretraining for fine-grained conditional computation without additional routing parameters.
Gated architectures beyond SwiGLU (e.g., Griffin's RG-LRU~\cite{de2024griffin}) produce analogous structured sparsity through their gating mechanisms; output-distribution prediction could potentially extend to such architectures, though architectural differences would require separate validation.
